summary: Retires the MD4 message digest algorithm described in RFC 1320 and explains the reasons, moving it to Historic status. It is informational.

eli5.summary: MD4 is an old fingerprinting recipe for data. Weaknesses were found, so this note says to stop using it.

subtitle: Why the MD4 hash algorithm was retired and RFC 1320 moved to Historic status.

tldr.problem: MD4, published in 1992, has been under attack for years, and collisions and pre-images can now be found cheaply, yet it still appeared in various protocols.
tldr.mechanism: The document reviews the attacks, lists the RFCs that reference MD4 and the effect on each, and moves RFC 1320 to Historic status.
tldr.outcome: MD4 should be replaced by an existing hash algorithm such as SHA-256. The one notable impact is Microsoft's use of MD4 in RC4-HMAC.

facts.label: Key size not to hash with MD4

today: RFC 6150 moves RFC 1320 to Historic status and is itself Informational, with no later RFC obsoleting or updating it in the unit metadata. It recommends SHA-256 or another existing hash algorithm instead of MD4.

sections.title: Retiring MD4
sections.content:
MD4 is a message digest algorithm that takes a message of arbitrary length and produces a 128-bit "fingerprint" or "message digest". RFC 6150 moves RFC 1320 to Historic status and discusses the reasons. As in its companion document on MD2, it assumes the reader is familiar with RFC 4270.

MD4 has been under attack since shortly after publication. In 1996 RSA suggested that it should not be used, and Microsoft made similar statements.
sections.eli5: MD4 squeezes any data into a short fingerprint. It has been broken for a long time, so this note retires it.

sections.title: Who Used MD4 and What Changes
sections.content:
MD4 was specified in an Internet Standard (RFC 2289, a one-time password system), a Draft Standard (RFC 1629), a Proposed Standard (RFC 3961, Kerberos 5 encryption and checksums), a BCP (RFC 4086) and several Informational RFCs. The impact of moving it to Historic is called minimal, with one exception.

  • One-time passwords have ostensibly been replaced by the HMAC-based mechanism of RFC 4226.
  • IDRP carried a 16-octet MD4 hash in each message; IDRP was replaced by BGP-4, which required at least MD5.
  • Kerberos 5 specified MD4 for DES encryption and checksum types; these were never really used and are being deprecated. Its mandatory-to-implement types use AES-256 and HMAC-SHA1.
  • The PKCS #1 versions 2.0 and 2.1 recommend against MD4. S/KEY implementations have started to use MD5 in place of MD4.

The exception is Microsoft's use of MD4 in MS-CHAP v1 and v2 and in RC4-HMAC, which are very widely deployed. RC4-HMAC, supported in Windows 2000 and later for backwards compatibility, does not rely on MD4's collision resistance. It uses MD4 to derive a key from a password, which is then used as input to HMAC-MD5, and key recovery attacks on HMAC-MD5 are not yet practical according to RFC 6151. In 2007, RFC 4962 listed both MS-CHAP versions as flawed. The rsync tool, which is not an IETF protocol, moved to MD5 in version 3.0.0 (2008).
sections.eli5: Only a few things still used MD4, and most had already switched. The big exception is some Microsoft login systems that still use it behind the scenes.

sections.title: What the Attacks Show
sections.content:
The document covers four kinds of weakness. For collisions, Dobbertin showed a practical attack in 1996 at 2^20 MD4 computations. In 2004 Xiaoyun Wang reduced this to 2^8 operations, and the document says she remarked that a collision can be found with a pen on a piece of paper.

For pre-images, the first attack on full MD4 had a complexity of 2^100. Improvements with some precomputation bring the pre-image and second pre-image costs to 2^78.4 and 2^69.4. The document says these attacks are practical, that MD4 cannot be used as a one-way function, and that it must not be used to hash a cryptographic key of 80 bits or longer.

For HMAC, the best published key recovery attack on HMAC-MD4 needs 2^72 queries and 2^77 MD4 computations.
sections.eli5: Making two files share a fingerprint is now so easy it can be done by hand, and working backwards from a fingerprint is feasible too.

sections.title: The Recommendation
sections.content:
Even though MD4 saw some deployment on the Internet, the document obsoletes it. MD4 is not a reasonable candidate for further standardization and should be deprecated in favor of existing hash algorithms such as SHA-256. RSA Security considers it appropriate to move MD4 to Historic status.

Deploying and withdrawing cryptography both take years, so algorithms need to be withdrawn before a catastrophic break is found. MD4 is already clearly showing weakness, and implementations should strongly consider removing support and migrating to another hash algorithm.
sections.eli5: Swapping out an old lock takes a long time, so you should do it while it is only weak and before it has been broken into.
